In the absence of knowledge of circumstances to the contrary, a debt collector shall assume that the convenient time for communicating with a consumer is after and before , local time at the consumers location ; ( 2 ) if the debt collector knows the consumer is represented by an attorney with respect to such debt and has knowledge of, or can readily ascertain, such attorneys name and address, unless the attorney fails to respond within a reasonable period of time to a communication from the debt collector or unless the attorney consents to direct communication with the consumer; or ( 3 ) at the consumers place of employment if the debt collector knows or has reason to know that the consumers employer prohibits the consumer from receiving such communication. ( b ) Communication with third parties Except as provided in section 1692b of this title, without the prior consent of the consumer given directly to the debt collector, or the express permission of a court of competent jurisdiction, or as reasonably necessary to effectuate a postjudgment judicial remedy, a debt collector may not communicate, in connection with the collection of any debt, with any person other than the consumer, his attorney, a consumer reporting agency if otherwise permitted by law, the creditor, the attorney of the creditor, or the attorney of the debt collector. ( c ) Ceasing communication If a consumer notifies a debt collector in writing that the consumer refuses to pay a debt or that the consumer wishes the debt collector to cease further communication with the consumer, the debt collector shall not communicate further with the consumer with respect to such debt, except ( 1 ) to advise the consumer that the debt collectors further efforts are being terminated ; ( 2 ) to notify the consumer that the debt collector or creditor may invoke specified remedies which are ordinarily invoked by such debt collector or creditor; or ( 3 ) where applicable, to notify the consumer that the debt collector or creditor intends to invoke a specified remedy. If such notice from the consumer is made by mail, notification shall be complete upon receipt. ( d ) Consumer defined For the purpose of this section, the term consumer includes the consumers spouse, parent ( if the consumer is a minor ), guardian, executor, or administrator.

narrative: I have a Chase Freedom Unlimited credit card. Chase offers a payment plan for large purchases ( over $100.00 ). The feature is called Pay Over Time and its info is here : Basically its a small loan that you pay over time for an individual purchase and the balance of that loan does not trigger interest/fees on your credit card as if you had a balance that you just hadn't paid. To activate this service you go to your chase account, look through your purchases and some of them will have an indication that they are eligible for pay over time. I have used this service once for a large medical bill last year. It had interest. I paid it off early. Easy-peasy. I am about to incur a series of very large medical expenses next week totaling $10000.00. It is for a medical treatment that is not being covered by my insurance but is medically necessary. I am interested in finding ways to finance those charges. The doctor sent me info for a company called that provides % APR loans for medical purchases but I looked at the reviews and they were scathing. I don't want to get caught up in a scam with a shady bank. So I thought about Chase 's Pay Over Time option. I wanted to know IN ADVANCE if my purchases at my doctors office would be eligible for the pay over time feature with % interest because payment is due in advance of each day of treatment next week. I need to know if I can use this service in this way or if I need to arrange for another payment option such as or another bank. I called Chase and asked for this information, at first they said " Oh we understand why you want to know, unfortunately there is no way to know in advance if a purchase will be eligible '' this was unacceptable to me so I spoke to an account supervisor. She said the same thing. When I asked her " Well it can't be random these determinations have to be made according to a policy. '' She said " It is random sir, we even don't know thats why we tell people to never expect a purchase to be offered eligibility to that pay over time feature. '' I even asked, since I will have identical charges of $2000.00, if of them is offered pay over time if it will be guaranteed the other ones will as well, provided that the vendor is the same, the customer is the same, and the total amount does not exceed the credit limit of the card? The supervisor said " Its not a guarantee, I've seen it where people in this situation are given pay over time for some of these, but not all, and sometimes none. '' I said I'd like to file a complaint because this kind of opacity in offering what is essentially a loan isn't above board. I filed a complaint. Now I am reporting this to you because of the following concerns : . Lack of consumer transparency into financial services . Any time a financial services company says determination is " random '' or algorithmic, it is a recipe for discrimination and price fixing . The fact that customers cant make financial decisions with all the facts ahead of time is a guarantee that some people are going to misinterpret the tool and get trapped in bad financial predicaments . There is a legal definition of a loan, there are legal requirements for conditions of loans. I am concerned that these pay over time options are essentially loans, but the idea that they are being offered after purchase makes them able to fall outside of the traditional definition of a loan and thus skirt legal requirements for loan conditions. Those loan conditions are there for a reason. . On the whole it seems pretty shady and I trust that professionals in the CFPB will have the experience and expertise to extrapolate why this practice is problematic for consumers.

Under Regulation Z 1026.9 ( c ), creditors are required to provide advance written notice of significant changes in account terms that may adversely affect the consumer. A post-hoc email notification does not satisfy this requirement. Additionally, I did not receive a timely adverse action notice identifying the specific reasons for the credit limit reduction or the principal factors relied upon, as required when credit is materially reduced. The timing and absence of advance notice prevented me from anticipating or mitigating the negative impact on my credit profile. I am submitting this complaint due to the lack of advance notice, the absence of timely adverse-action disclosures, and the material harm caused by the immediate increase in utilization following a payment.

Their reply, dated does not adequately address the legal and factual basis of my dispute and fails to support continued credit reporting of a charge-off stemming from a legally dismissed case. 1. The Charge-Off Is Based on a Dismissed Case Navy Federal confirmed that the lawsuit tied to this account was dismissed without prejudice on due to failure to serve ( Case No. ). The case was only re-filed in and is still pending. At the time the charge-off was reported, there was no enforceable judgment or active debt claim. Reporting a final charge-off while pursuing the debt in a separate legal action misrepresents the debt status and violates the accuracy requirement of the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( B ). 2. The Reporting is Inaccurate and Inconsistent The charge-off is inconsistently reported across Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion. Some months are listed as paid, others late, with incorrect or mismatched dates. This violates the duty to report information that is not only accurate but complete and consistent, per 15 U.S.C. 1681i ( a ). See ) and ) furnishers must perform reasonable investigations, not just assert correctness based on internal records. 3. Delayed Response Undermines Reasonableness Navy Federal waited nearly days to issue a final response. While technically within CFPB limits, this extended delay without resolving the clear legal questions raises concerns about the timeliness and reasonableness of their investigation, as required under 15 U.S.C. 1681i ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ). 4. The Account Should Be Removed Pending Legal Resolution Since the case is still in litigation and no court judgment has established legal responsibility, continuing to report a final charge-off causes unjustified credit damage. Navy Federal should not report this item as settled, resolved, or final while also pursuing the debt in court. This is prejudicial and misleading, especially under the FCRA and general principles of fair credit reporting.

narrative: CFPB Complaint American Express Product : Credit Card Issue : Credit limit reduction with inadequate notice causing cascading harm across multiple credit accounts Company : American Express Account : Ending in Member Since : ( 18 years ) Narrative I have been an American Express since over years. Throughout that period, I maintained an excellent payment history, frequently paying my balance weekly or multiple times per month. My was high, and I had a $20000.00 credit limit with utilization consistently under 25 %. In my contract position was unexpectedly cut short. I secured new employment by approximately During that brief gap, I relied on my credit cards for essential expenses which is precisely the purpose credit products are designed to serve. When I started my new job, I incurred additional work-related expenses that required reimbursement through my employers expense report process. Because the new employer used a manual, paper-based system, reimbursement took significantly longer than expected. On American Express sent me an email stating they were reviewing my credit limit and demanding a payment of $2100.00 by a window of just calendar days to avoid a credit limit reduction. This timeframe was wholly inadequate. It did not allow for standard brokerage settlement periods ( typically business days ) to liquidate assets, nor did it account for the reality that a working person can not always arrange a significant payment in hours. On American Express reduced my credit limit from $20000.00 to $8900.00 a 55 % reduction. My cash advance limit was reduced to $200.00. The This single action by American Express triggered a devastating cascade. Because my utilization ratio on this card spiked dramatically ( from under 25 % to a much higher percentage on a now-smaller limit ), other credit issuers automated risk systems flagged the change and followed suit : On reduced credit limit on a card I have held since ( account ending ). On reduced my credit limit on a second card ( account ending ). I did not miss payments on any of these accounts. The only trigger was the utilization ratio change caused by American Expresss initial reduction. The result : I went from manageable, low-utilization balances across multiple cards to being near maximum on all of them not because I increased my spending, but because the available credit underneath my existing balances was removed. My minimum monthly payments increased from approximately $300.00 to over $1000.00. I lost access to 0 % interest balance transfer offers that could have helped me manage the situation. By the time my expense reimbursement arrived, I needed it entirely for the new, higher minimum payments. On American Express sent another email demanding a payment of $1300.00 by again, just calendar days or they will reduce my credit limit further. I called American Express and explained the full situation. The representative acknowledged my ears of membership and thanked me for my loyalty, but stated there was nothing she could do and that the only option was to watch and see if they lower my limit again. I explained that days is insufficient to liquidate investments ( brokerage settlements take business days ), and was told nothing could be done. Why This Is Unfair I am not asking for special treatment. I am asking the CFPB to examine whether American Expresss practice of issuing ultimatums that trigger cascading credit damage across a consumers entire credit profile constitutes an unfair practice under UDAAP ( Unfair, Deceptive, or Abusive Acts or Practices ). The harm to me was substantial and unavoidable. I could not reasonably prevent it within the notice period given. American Expresss action did not just reduce my limit on their card it destroyed my credit utilization ratio across all accounts, triggering automatic reductions by other issuers and converting what was a temporary, manageable situation into an ongoing financial burden. Credit cards exist to bridge temporary financial gaps. I used mine for their intended purpose, maintained payments throughout, and was punished with a self-reinforcing cycle of limit reductions that no amount of responsible behavior could stop. sub_product: General-purpose credit card or charge card
sub_issue: Charged too much interest
narrative: I enabled shortly after opening my Chase Sapphire credit card. During the setup process, the default selection was Minimum payment due. The interface did not provide any clear or conspicuous warning that choosing the default option would cause the account to continue accruing daily interest. The screen also did not disclose that selecting minimum payment would result in carrying a balance and incurring finance charges. The Payment definitions section within the same interface also did not mention interest accrual or any financial consequences of choosing the minimum-payment option. Because there was no clear disclosure, I reasonably believed that enabling would help avoid additional charges. As a result, I unknowingly incurred purchase interest for multiple billing cycles. I contacted customer service and later spoke with a supervisor. They confirmed that the interest was due to being set to minimum payment but declined to make any adjustments. I believe this issue involves potential problems with disclosure and default settings : Potential TILA / Regulation Z disclosure deficiency The interface did not clearly disclose that selecting minimum payment in would cause finance charges to accrue. Disclosure regarding a consumers financial obligation must be clear and conspicuous under Regulation Z. Potential UDAAP concern ( Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices ) The design places minimum payment as the default option without warning of the financial consequences. Presenting a default option that leads to continued interest accrual, without adequate disclosure, may be considered a misleading omission. Lack of clear warning for a material financial term Interest accrual from carrying a balance is a material finance term. The interface did not provide a warning that choosing minimum payment would result in interest charges, which may fail the reasonable-consumer standard. I am not originally from the U.S. and did not have prior experience with U.S. credit card systems before coming here. Because of this, the default setting and lack of disclosure were not intuitive, and I relied on the interface to understand my obligations. I have attached screenshots showing the interface and the lack of clear disclosure.

narrative: I am submitting a complaint regarding the handling of a credit card dispute by Goldman Sachs Bank USA Apple Card ) involving a $5500.00 charge dated with the merchant listed as Fanbasis * Bogegroup. Prior to making this payment, I was informed by the merchant that, after reviewing my outstanding FICO scores and business goals, I hadqualified for an interest-free line of credit, which led me to believe that financing had effectively been preliminarily approved or arranged. However, after the payment was made, I received written instructions from the merchant directing me to take additional steps that had not been disclosed beforehand. Specifically, I was instructed to : Apply for a new credit card ( that would have been my third ) ; Open three separate business checking accounts ( ) ; Deposit approximately $2500.00 $3000.00 into each account ( totaling approximately $7500.00 $9000.00 ) ; Continue applying for additional credit cards as part of a funding plan. The written communication stated that these steps were necessary to build banking relationships for higher approvals in the next round of funding. This indicated that no line of credit had actually been approved at the time payment was requested, despite prior representations that I had qualified for such credit. These instructions raised not only financial concerns for me but also fundamental ethical concerns, as they required establishing multiple new banking relationships and depositing substantial funds that I did not previously have. These requirements were not disclosed prior to payment and are not reflected in the written agreement provided to me. Before disputing the charge, I contacted the merchant and requested that these newly introduced requirements be withdrawn so that I could proceed under the terms I believed I had agreed to. My message indicated that I was willing to continue if those conditions were removed. When I received no response, I requested that the transaction be canceled and my payment refunded. I then disputed the charge with Goldman Sachs. A provisional credit was initially issued and later reversed. After I requested reconsideration, Goldman Sachs again denied the dispute, stating that there was no evidence to substantiate my claim. I subsequently reviewed the merchants chargeback submission provided to Goldman Sachs. That submission does not disclose that, after payment, I was instructed to open multiple bank accounts and deposit approximately $7500.00 $9000.00 as part of a funding plan, nor does it address the representation that I had qualified for a line of credit prior to payment. As a result, I believe that Goldman Sachs evaluated the dispute based on incomplete information and did not consider the full circumstances of the transaction. I propose a fair resolution to this matter that would include : Reinstatement of the $5500.00 credit to my Apple Card account and removal of any associated interest or fees ; Confirmation that no negative credit reporting related to this matter will remain ; Written disclosure of the documentation relied upon in denying my dispute, including the merchants chargeback submission and identification of the legal merchant of record. This dispute arises from a material difference between what I understood I was purchasing and what was required after payment. Had these additional requirements been disclosed in advance, I would not have agreed to proceed.

Information about applicable regulations currently in effect can be found at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau 's website, consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. NOTICE TO FURNISHERS OF INFORMATION : OBLIGATIONS OF FURNISHERS UNDER THE FCRA The federal Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), 15 U.S.C. 1681-1681y, imposes responsibilities on all persons who furnish information to consumer reporting agencies ( CRAs ). These responsibilities are found in Section 623 of the FCRA, 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2. State law may impose additional requirements on furnishers. All furnishers of information to CRAs should become familiar with the applicable laws and may want to consult with their counsel to ensure that they are in compliance. The text of the FCRA is set forth in full at the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection 's website at consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. A list of the sections of the FCRA cross-referenced to the U.S. Code is at the end of this document. Section 623 imposes the following duties : Accuracy Guidelines The banking and credit union regulators and the CFPB will promulgate guidelines and regulations dealing with the accuracy of information provided to CRAs by furnishers. The regulations and guidelines issued by the CFPB will be available at consumerfinance.gov/learnmore when they are issued. Section 623 ( e ). General Prohibition on Reporting Inaccurate Information The FCRA prohibits information furnishers from providing information to a CRA that they know or have reasonable cause to believe is inaccurate. However, the furnisher is not subject to this general prohibition if it clearly and conspicuously specifies an address to which consumers may write to notify the furnisher that certain information is inaccurate. Sections 623 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ) and ( a ) ( 1 ) ( C ). Duty to Correct and Update Information If at any time a person who regularly and in the ordinary course of business furnishes information to one or more CRAs determines that the information provided is not complete or accurate, the furnisher must promptly provide complete and accurate information to the CRA. In addition, the furnisher must notify all CRAs that received the information of any corrections, and must thereafter report only the complete and accurate information. Section 623 ( a ) ( 2 ). Duties After Notice of Dispute from Consumer If a consumer notifies a furnisher, at an address specified by the furnisher for such notices, that specific information is inaccurate, and the information is, in fact, inaccurate, the furnisher must thereafter report the correct information to CRAs. Section 623 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( B ). If a consumer notifies a furnisher that the consumer disputes the completeness or accuracy of any information reported by the furnisher, the furnisher may not subsequently report that information to a CRA without providing notice of the dispute. Section 623 ( a ) ( 3 ). The federal banking and credit union regulators and the CFPB will issue regulations that will identify when an information furnisher must investigate a dispute made directly to the furnisher by a consumer. Once these regulations are issued, furnishers must comply with them and complete an investigation within 30 days ( or 45 days, if the consumer later provides relevant additional information ) unless the dispute is frivolous or irrelevant or comes from a credit repair organization. The CFPB regulations will be available at consumerfinance.gov. Section 623 ( a ) ( 8 ). Duties After Notice of Dispute from Consumer Reporting Agency If a CRA notifies a furnisher that a consumer disputes the completeness or accuracy of information provided by the furnisher, the furnisher has a duty to follow certain procedures. The furnisher must : Conduct an investigation and review all relevant information provided by the CRA, including information given to the CRA by the consumer. Sections 623 ( b ) ( 1 ) ( A ) and ( b ) ( 1 ) ( B ). Report the results to the CRA that referred the dispute, and, if the investigation establishes that the information was, in fact, incomplete or inaccurate, report the results to all CRAs to which the furnisher provided the information that compile and maintain files on a nationwide basis. Sections 623 ( b ) ( 1 ) ( C ) and ( b ) ( 1 ) ( D ). Complete the above steps within 30 days from the date the CRA receives the dispute ( or 45 days, if the consumer later provides relevant additional information to the CRA ). Section 623 ( b ) ( 2 ). Promptly modify or delete the information, or block its reporting. Section 623 ( b ) ( 1 ) ( E ). Duty to Report Voluntary Closing of Credit Accounts If a consumer voluntarily closes a credit account, any person who regularly and in the ordinary course of business furnishes information to one or more CRAs must report this fact when it provides information to CRAs for the time period in which the account was closed. Section 623 ( a ) ( 4 ). Duty to Report Dates of Delinquencies If a furnisher reports information concerning a delinquent account placed for collection, charged to profit or loss, or subject to any similar action, the furnisher must, within 90 days after reporting the information, provide the CRA with the month and the year of the commencement of the delinquency that immediately preceded the action, so that the agency will know how long to keep the information in the consumer 's file. Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ). Any person, such as a debt collector, that has acquired or is responsible for collecting delinquent accounts and that reports information to CRAs may comply with the requirements of Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ) ( until there is a consumer dispute ) by reporting the same delinquency date previously reported by the creditor. If the creditor did not report this date, they may comply with the FCRA by establishing reasonable procedures to obtain and report delinquency dates, or, if a delinquency date can not be reasonably obtained, by following reasonable procedures to ensure that the date reported precedes the date when the account was placed for collection, charged to profit or loss, or subjected to any similar action. Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ). Duties of Financial Institutions When Reporting Negative Information Financial institutions that furnish information to nationwide consumer reporting agencies, as defined in Section 603 ( p ), must notify consumers in writing if they may furnish or have furnished negative information to a CRA. Section 623 ( a ) ( 7 ). The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has prescribed model disclosures, 12 CFR Part 1022, App. B. Duties When Furnishing Medical Information A furnisher whose primary business is providing medical services, products, or devices ( and such furnisher 's agents or assignees ) is a medical information furnisher for the purposes of the FCRA and must notify all CRAs to which it reports of this fact. Section 623 ( a ) ( 9 ). This notice will enable CRAs to comply with their duties under Section 604 ( g ) when reporting medical information. Duties when ID Theft Occurs All furnishers must have in place reasonable procedures to respond to notifications from CRAs that information furnished is the result of identity theft, and to prevent refurnishing the information in the future. A furnisher may not furnish information that a consumer has identified as resulting from identity theft unless the furnisher subsequently knows or is informed by the consumer that the information is correct. Section 623 ( a ) ( 6 ). If a furnisher learns that it has furnished inaccurate information due to identity theft, it must notify each consumer reporting agency of the correct information and must thereafter report only complete and accurate information. Section 623 ( a ) ( 2 ). When any furnisher of information is notified pursuant to the procedures set forth in Section 605B that a debt has resulted from identity theft, the furnisher may not sell, transfer, or place for collection the debt except in certain limited circumstances. Section 615 ( f ). The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau website, consumerfinance.gov/learnmore, has more information about the FCRA. Failure to Provide IRS Form 1099-C : Under IRS regulations ( 26 U.S. Code 6050P ), financial institutions are required to file Form 1099-C with the IRS and provide a copy to the borrower when a debt of $600.00 or more is canceled or forgiven.
